speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. To help me understand your dizziness and vertigo, could you describe exactly what the sensation feels like? Is it a spinning sensation of the room around you, or more of a feeling of lightheadedness or imbalance?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any ringing in your ears (tinnitus) or hearing changes specifically during these dizzy episodes? Also, how long does each spell of vertigo typically last?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the dizziness start immediately when you roll over in bed, look up, or bend down, and does each episode last for less than a minute? I also need to know if you have experienced any recent head trauma or neck injury.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical or surgical history. No history of Meniere's disease, vestibular neuritis, or labyrinthitis. Social history: Retired school teacher. Lives alone. Non-smoker, occasional wine. Enjoys light gardening.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any nausea, vomiting, or visual disturbances like double vision during these episodes? Also, have you noticed any weakness or numbness in your face, arms, or legs?

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headache, tinnitus, hearing loss, nausea, vomiting, or recent respiratory infections.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the positional nature of your vertigo and the absence of other neurological or auditory symptoms, I suspect Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo. REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike maneuver

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Positive for right-sided horizontal nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine position, suggestive of BPPV

speaker: Doctor
text:
The Dix-Hallpike test confirms right-sided benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. I will now perform the Epley maneuver to reposition the displaced otoconia and relieve your symptoms.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
